newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU prods Japan on leather and film trade policies.
newsitem.headline: EU prods Japan on leather and film trade policies.

text.p: The European Union weighed into Japanese trade policies on Tuesday, criticising Tokyo both for its domestic market for photographic film and its alleged import restrictions on finished leather products.

Two European Commission statements said the EU had presented its views about film to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Geneva and announced an own-initiative inquiry into the Japanese market for finished leather products.

"The EU has a direct export interest in the Japanese consumer film market, and shares U.S. concerns at the difficulties encountered when distributing consumer photographic film and paper in Japan," said one statement.

"The EU is anxious to see fair competitive conditions established and preserved in the Japanese film market for imports and domestic products alike, and believes imports are put at a disadvantage by Japanese government measures in breach of WTO rules," it added.
Japan rejected U.S. charges of market-fixing when it addressed a WTO dispute panel earlier this month.
Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd, the Japanese firm in the row, said at the time that Washington's case on behalf of Eastman Kodak Co would be "totally and decisively refuted" by the panel.
Kodak, whose long-standing complaint concerns what it sees as Tokyo's unfair marketing rules, cites as evidence its 70 percent home market share compared with nine percent in Japan.

The Commission said its leather probe came after complaints by the European tanning industry about high Japanese import tariffs and the "dissuasive management of quotas, domestic price fixing and subsidies to domestic producers".

European tanners, represented by the Confederation of National Associations of Tanners and Dressers of the EU, said they faced penalties of up to 270 percent of the import cost of raw hide in order to sell finished leather imports in Japan.

The result was that such imports had just two percent of the Japanese market, said the Commission, adding that its probe "could lead to a challenge before the WTO if Japan does not give a statisfactory response".
